title: Fix it: parse a fixed-width payroll extract
prompt:
The script in the editor is **almost** right. It passes on the sample and fails on a case you cannot see.

The original task was:

A mainframe payroll job writes one line per employee, with no delimiters between fields — every field sits at a fixed character position:

| field | start (0-based) | length |
|---|---|---|
| id | 0 | 6 |
| name | 6 | 20 |
| salary | 26 | 10 |
| dept | 36 | 3 |

`name` is space-padded on the right to fill its width. `salary` is zero-padded on the left and always has exactly two decimal digits, for example `0004250.00`. Lines are separated by `\n`, and the file may contain blank lines.

Return an array of `{ id, name, salary, dept }`, one per non-blank line, with `name` and `dept` trimmed and `salary` as a Number.

Find what is wrong and fix it. You can press Run to see what it currently does.
hints: Run it on the sample first. If the sample looks right, the bug only shows on data the sample does not contain.
Ask what kind of input would break this — an empty list, a missing field, a value ordered differently.
declares the name field one column short (19 instead of 20); harmless on a short name, but silently truncates a name that exactly fills the column

explanation.approach: There is no reader for this format here — application/flatfile in this engine requires a schema resource loaded from the classpath, and passing one inline as a reader property does not satisfy it (it fails with 'No schema set' no matter what the property is named). So the file arrives as inputMime text/plain, a single String, and the parsing is manual: split on newlines, then pull each field out of a line with a range selector at a fixed offset. The two ways this goes wrong without an error are a field width that is off by one, and a blank line that survives the split.

snippets.label: The payload is a plain String here, not a parsed structure
snippets.note: splitBy on the raw text gives an array of line Strings. Nothing has been parsed into fields yet.

snippets.label: A range selector plus trim pulls one field out
snippets.note: line[6 to 25] is the 20-character name column, spaces and all. trim removes the padding — it does not know or care where the padding came from.

snippets.label: A parsed field is still a String until you say otherwise
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  raw: "E00001Alice Chen          0004250.00ENG"[26 to 35],
  rawType: typeOf("E00001Alice Chen          0004250.00ENG"[26 to 35]),
  asNumber: "E00001Alice Chen          0004250.00ENG"[26 to 35] as Number
}
snippets.note: The salary column comes out as the String "0004250.00". as Number drops the leading zeros and keeps the cents — 4250, not a display string.

snippets.label: Why application/flatfile is not the answer here
snippets.note: This is the built-in flat-file reader, and it looks like the right tool. It throws IllegalStateException: No schema set regardless of what the schema property is called or shaped — this engine expects the schema as a classpath resource, which a headless practice script has no way to supply. Range selectors on a String are the fallback that actually works.

snippets.label: One column short is silent, not an error
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
var layout = [ { name: "name", start: 6, length: 19 } ]
fun field(line, start, length) = trim(line[start to (start + length - 1)])
---
field("E00002Bartholomew Chen III0001500.75SAL", 6, 19)
snippets.note: r2's name is exactly 20 characters — "Bartholomew Chen III" — with no padding to spare. Reading only 19 of them drops the trailing "I" and returns a different, still-plausible-looking name. No exception, no null — just a wrong answer, and only on the one row with no slack in it.

snippets.label: A blank line fails later than you'd expect
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
("" splitBy "\n") map (line) -> line[26 to 35] as Number
snippets.note: An empty line has no character at position 26 — the selector returns null, and null as Number throws UnsupportedTypeCoercionException. The failure surfaces at the coercion, several steps after the split that actually produced the bad element, which is why filtering blank lines up front is easier than debugging this backward.
